opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's exciting because, for the first time, the tools we've been building in machine learning are actually good enough to bite into the hard problems in the physical sciences. I started out as a physicist, and I moved into machine learning partly because it felt like the place where the real action was. Now the two worlds are coming back together, and it feels a bit like coming home.

What's changed is that we can now build models that respect the structure of the physical world: symmetries, equivariance, conservation laws. That's a lot of what my group worked on over the years. Then you combine that with enormous amounts of compute and simulation data. You can learn force fields that are nearly as accurate as quantum chemistry but orders of magnitude faster. You can generate candidate molecules or materials instead of searching for them blindly. You can close the loop with experiments in the lab. That's a fundamentally different way of doing science.

There's also a deeper reason. Language models and image models have been trained on the internet, and at some point you run out of that data. Nature, though, is an infinite source of data. You can simulate it, you can measure it, and it doesn't lie to you the way internet text sometimes does. So I actually think the next big wave of AI will be grounded in the physical world. It will be about designing better batteries, better catalysts for carbon capture, and better drugs.

And frankly, the stakes are very high. Climate change, energy, sustainable materials, health — these are problems where we desperately need to speed up discovery. If AI can compress a materials discovery cycle that used to take ten or twenty years into one or two, that's not just a nice academic result. That could really change the trajectory we're on as a civilization. So, to me, this is the most meaningful thing I could be working on right now.

r001.rationale: The response says machine-learning models can now respect physical structure and combine with compute and simulation data to accelerate molecule and materials discovery, changing how science is done.

r002.rationale: The response expresses excitement about AI and science converging, but does not clearly attribute that excitement to the field being unexplored.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. You know, I've spent most of my career in machine learning, and before that I was actually trained as a physicist, so for me this convergence feels a little bit like coming home. For a long time these were two separate worlds. Scientists did science, and machine learning people built classifiers for images or language. But in the last few years something has really shifted. The models have gotten good enough, and the data has gotten rich enough, that we can start to apply these tools to the hardest problems in physics, chemistry, and biology, and get results that actually matter.

I think the reason it's so exciting is that science is, in some sense, the ultimate application. If you improve an ad-ranking model by a few percent, that's nice, but if you can predict how a protein folds, or discover a new material for carbon capture, or simulate a molecule accurately enough that you don't have to synthesize a thousand candidates in the lab, you're potentially changing the trajectory of entire fields. The feedback loop is also beautiful. Science gives us structure, symmetries, conservation laws, all this prior knowledge that we can bake into our models. And in return machine learning gives science a way to deal with complexity that was simply intractable before. Think about quantum chemistry. The exact equations have been known for almost a hundred years, but solving them scales terribly. Now we can learn approximations that are both fast and accurate.

And honestly, there's a philosophical dimension too. For centuries, the way we did science was to find a compact set of equations and reason from there. Now we're adding a second mode, where the model itself becomes the theory in a way, learned from data, maybe not human-interpretable in the traditional sense, but predictive. I find that genuinely fascinating. We're not replacing the scientific method, we're expanding what it can reach. So yes, I think this is one of those rare moments where the tools and the problems are finally matched, and I wanted to be right in the middle of it.

r001.rationale: The response says recent modeling advances make it possible to tackle previously intractable scientific problems and expand what scientific methods can reach.

r002.rationale: The response expresses enthusiasm about the convergence and its potential, but does not identify it as an unexplored field or attribute the enthusiasm to that quality.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that this goes in both directions. AI gives us new tools for doing science, and science gives us principles for building better AI.

In science, we’re constantly trying to infer something we can’t directly observe from measurements that are noisy or incomplete. That’s a very natural setting for machine learning. You can imagine learning models that help us simulate a physical system, explore possible molecules, or decide which experiment to do next. That can really accelerate the cycle of discovery.

But we also know a lot about these systems already. We have symmetries, conservation laws, and physical constraints. If we build that knowledge into a model, it doesn’t have to learn everything from scratch. And that’s an interesting scientific question in itself: how do you combine what you know with what you can learn from data?

For me, the exciting possibility is that AI becomes part of that loop between theory and experiment—helping us make predictions, test them, and ultimately understand something new.

r001.rationale: The response describes learned models for simulating physical systems, exploring molecules, and choosing experiments as tools that can accelerate scientific discovery.

r002.rationale: The response expresses excitement about AI and science, but does not attribute it to opportunities in an unexplored field.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that AI is becoming a tool for scientific discovery. We can use it to build models of complex systems, explore possible explanations, and help decide which experiment to do next. That creates a feedback loop: you learn from data, make a prediction, test it, and improve the model.

And the exchange goes both ways. Science gives AI powerful principles—symmetries, conservation laws, uncertainty—that help us build models that need less data and generalize better. You don’t want to learn everything from scratch when you already know something about how the world works.

So there’s a tremendous opportunity here: combining what we know with what we can learn from data, to tackle problems that have been very difficult to solve with either approach alone.

r001.rationale: It says AI can model complex systems, explore explanations, and guide experiments, creating a data-and-testing feedback loop for scientific discovery.

r002.rationale: The response expresses excitement about opportunities from combining scientific knowledge with data, but does not identify the field as unexplored.
